curriculum.title: HTML Tags and Style Basics
curriculum.description: A detailed curriculum for absolute beginners where avatar text carries the main lesson explanations for HTML tags, elements, attributes, CSS selectors, and styles.

avatar.intro_template: Welcome! In this lesson, you will learn about {{lesson_title}}.
avatar.start_questions_prompt: When you are ready, click Start Questions.
avatar.handoff_to_practice: Now it is your turn. Try the tiny code challenge.
avatar.lesson_complete_template: Nice work! In this lesson, you learned about {{lesson_title}}.
avatar.incorrect_feedback: Almost. Let's try that one more time.

lessons.title: Tags
lessons.goal: Understand what an HTML tag is and use heading tags to make a page title.

avatar.text: Hello, web builder. Today we will meet HTML tags. Tags are small instructions that help a browser build a web page.

flow.title: What is an HTML tag?
flow.body:
An HTML tag is an instruction for the browser. Tags help the browser make page pieces such as: - Headings - Paragraphs - Images - Buttons Most tags are written with angle brackets around a tag name. Example opening tag: `

` Example closing tag: `

`

avatar.text: An HTML tag is an instruction for the browser. A tag tells the browser what kind of page piece to make. We will use a heading tag to make a big page title as our first example.

flow.title: A heading tag makes a title
flow.body:
The `h1` tag makes the biggest heading on a page. A complete heading element has three parts: 1. Opening tag: `

` 2. Words: `My Page` 3. Closing tag: `

` Full example: `

My Page

`

avatar.text: The heading tag makes a large title. First we start the heading by putting h1 between the opening and closing angle brackets. Next we add the title words. Then we close the heading. The closing heading tag is the same as the opening tag, but it adds a slash before the tag name. Study the code example next to see how the pieces fit together.

code_example.description: One main heading element.
code_example.explanation: The h1 opening tag starts the heading. My Page is the visible title. The closing tag ends the heading.

question.question: Which option is an opening heading tag?
question.explanation: The opening heading tag has the tag name h1 inside angle brackets.

avatar.on_ask: Choose the option that starts a heading.
avatar.on_correct: Correct. That is an opening heading tag.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the tag name h1 inside angle brackets.

question.question: Which option correctly closes a heading?
question.explanation: A closing tag uses the same tag name and adds a slash before the name.

avatar.on_ask: Choose the option that ends a heading.
avatar.on_correct: Correct. The slash shows that the heading is ending.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the heading tag with a slash before the name.

question.question: Write one main heading that says My Page.
question.explanation: Great work. The title words belong between the opening and closing heading tags.

code_example.description: A single main heading.
code_example.explanation: Use an opening h1 tag, add the words My Page, and finish with a closing h1 tag.

avatar.before_demo: Here is a small heading example.
avatar.handoff: Now build the heading by yourself.

points: A tag is an instruction for the browser
The h1 tag makes the main page heading
Many elements use an opening tag, words, and a closing tag

avatar.text: Nice work. You learned that tags guide the browser. You also used a heading tag to make a big title.
Next, we will learn how tags and words join together to make an HTML element.

lessons.title: Tags Make Elements
lessons.goal: Understand that tags and content can join together to make complete HTML elements.

avatar.text: You have met HTML tags. Now we will learn how tags and words join together to make a complete page piece.

flow.title: Tags become elements
flow.body:
An HTML element is a complete page piece made by the browser. Many elements have: 1. An opening tag 2. Content 3. A closing tag Example: `

Hello!

` Some elements, such as `img`, stand alone and do not need a closing tag.

avatar.text: An element is the full page piece. Many elements begin with an opening tag, hold some words, and finish with a closing tag.

flow.title: Element pieces fit together
flow.body:
Look at this paragraph element: `

I like coding.

` Its parts are: - Opening tag: `

` - Content: `I like coding.` - Closing tag: `

` The opening and closing tags use the same tag name. The closing tag adds a slash.

avatar.text: The opening tag starts the paragraph. The words are the content. The closing tag tells the browser that the paragraph is finished. Study the code example next to see how the pieces fit together.

code_example.description: A complete paragraph element.
code_example.explanation: The opening paragraph tag starts the element. The sentence is the content. The closing paragraph tag ends it.

question.question: Which option makes a complete element?
question.explanation: An element has the opening tag, content, and closing tag.

avatar.on_ask: Choose the tag that ends a paragraph.
avatar.on_correct: Correct. The slash shows that the paragraph is ending.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the paragraph tag that includes a slash.

question.question: Many HTML elements have an opening tag, content, and a closing tag.
question.explanation: Many HTML elements use these three parts to create one complete page piece.

avatar.on_ask: Is this statement true or false?
avatar.on_correct: Correct. Those three parts often make one complete element.
avatar.on_wrong: Think about the opening tag, the words, and the closing tag.

points: A tag is one part of an HTML element
An element is a complete page piece
Many elements have an opening tag, content, and a closing tag

avatar.text: You did it. Tags and content can work together to make a complete HTML element.
Next, we will use a paragraph element to add a friendly sentence to a page.

lessons.title: Paragraph
lessons.goal: Use the paragraph element to add a short sentence to a web page.

avatar.text: A web page needs words that explain ideas. A paragraph gives us a neat place for a short sentence.

flow.title: Paragraphs hold sentences
flow.body:
The `p` tag makes a paragraph. A paragraph is a small group of words or sentences. A complete paragraph has: 1. Opening tag: `

` 2. Sentence: `I like coding.` 3. Closing tag: `

` Full example: `

I like coding.

`

avatar.text: The paragraph tag holds a sentence. We start the paragraph, add the words, and then end the paragraph. Take a moment to look at the paragraph code example next for better understanding.

flow.title: Keep paragraph text clear
flow.body:
Paragraphs are useful for: - A short fact - A friendly message - A simple description Example: `

My robot can dance.

` The words shown on the page go between the opening and closing paragraph tags.

avatar.text: A paragraph can share one clear idea. Short sentences are a great place to begin. Look through the displayed information next to see the paragraph code example.

code_example.description: One short paragraph.
code_example.explanation: The paragraph opening tag starts the sentence area. The sentence is shown on the page. The closing tag ends the paragraph.

question.question: What does a paragraph element usually hold?
question.explanation: A paragraph usually holds words or sentences that explain an idea.

avatar.on_ask: What kind of content belongs in a paragraph?
avatar.on_correct: Correct. Paragraphs are useful for sentences.
avatar.on_wrong: Think about the element used for normal page words.

question.question: Write one paragraph that says I like coding.
question.explanation: Nice work. The sentence belongs between the opening and closing paragraph tags.

code_example.description: A single paragraph element.
code_example.explanation: Start a paragraph, add the sentence, and close the paragraph.

avatar.before_demo: Here is a short paragraph example.
avatar.handoff: Now write the paragraph by yourself.

points: The p tag makes a paragraph
Paragraphs hold words and sentences
The sentence goes between the opening and closing paragraph tags

avatar.text: Excellent. You can now add a clear sentence to a web page with a paragraph.
Next, we will add a picture with an image tag.

lessons.title: Image
lessons.goal: Use an image tag with source and alternative text attributes.

avatar.text: Pictures make web pages exciting. Today we will learn how an image tag tells the browser which picture to show.

flow.title: The image tag shows a picture
flow.body: An image tag uses: - `src` to name the picture file or URL - `alt` to describe the picture in words Example: ``

avatar.text: It is a void tag. This means it stands alone and does not need a closing tag. It needs a picture file name or URL and helpful words that describe the picture. Take a moment to look at the displayed information next for better understanding.

flow.title: Source and alternative text
flow.body: Look at this image tag: `` - `img` tells the browser to show an image - `src` gives the picture a file name or URL - `alt` gives helpful words about the picture The `alt` words are useful when the picture cannot be seen or loaded.

avatar.text: The source tells the browser which picture file or URL to use. The alternative text gives a clear description of that picture. Study the breakdown of the image tag, the source attribute and the alternative text next to see how the pieces fit together.

code_example.description: One image tag with source and alternative text.
code_example.explanation: The source attribute names the image file or URL. The alternative text describes the image. The image tag does not need a closing tag.

question.question: Which attribute names the picture file or URL?
question.explanation: The source attribute tells the browser which image file or URL to show.

avatar.on_ask: Which attribute chooses the picture?
avatar.on_correct: Correct. Source points to the picture file or URL.
avatar.on_wrong: Think of the word source.

question.question: Which attribute describes the picture in words?
question.explanation: The alternative text attribute gives a helpful description of the picture.

avatar.on_ask: Which attribute gives helpful picture words?
avatar.on_correct: Correct. Alternative text describes the picture.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the attribute used for a picture description.

question.question: Write one image tag for star URL with the description A yellow square with the word: Star.
question.explanation: Great work. The image tag includes the file name or URL and a helpful description.

code_example.description: A single image tag.
code_example.explanation: Use the source attribute for the file name or URL and the alternative text attribute for the description.
code_example.starterCode:
<!-- Write the img tag below and use this url for the source: https://rb.gy/qy871l 
and this for the alt text: A yellow square with the word: Star -->

avatar.before_demo: Here is a small image example.
avatar.handoff: Now build the image tag by yourself.

points: The img tag shows a picture
The img tag is a void tag and does not need a closing tag
The src attribute names the picture file
The alt attribute describes the picture in words

avatar.text: Fantastic. You can now add a picture and describe it with helpful words.
Next, we will make a button that looks ready to press.

lessons.title: Button
lessons.goal: Use the button element to make a simple pressable page piece.

avatar.text: Buttons invite people to take action. Today we will make a simple button with short and clear words.

flow.title: Buttons hold action words
flow.body:
The `button` tag makes a button.

A button holds short action words.

A complete button has:

1. Opening tag: `<button>`
2. Button words: `Press me`
3. Closing tag: `</button>`

Full example:

`<button>Press me</button>`

avatar.text: The button tag makes a button. A button usually holds short action words. We start the button, add the words people will see, and then end the button.

flow.title: Use clear button words
flow.body:
Good button words tell the learner what action to take.

Examples:

- `Start`
- `Play`
- `Continue`
- `Click me`

Example element:

`<button>Continue</button>`

avatar.text: Clear button words help people know what will happen next. Short words are easiest to read. Study the displayed information next to see some example words for buttons.

code_example.description: One button element.
code_example.explanation: The opening button tag starts the button. Click me is the visible button text. The closing button tag ends the element.

question.question: Which words make a clear beginner button?
options: A very long story about buttons
question.explanation: Click me is short, clear, and tells the learner what action to take.

avatar.on_ask: Choose the clearest button words.
avatar.on_correct: Correct. Short action words work well on buttons.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the short action message.

question.question: Write one button that says Click me.
question.explanation: Great work. The button words belong between the opening and closing button tags.

code_example.description: A single button element.
code_example.explanation: Start the button, add the words Click me, and close the button.

avatar.before_demo: Here is a simple button example.
avatar.handoff: Now build the button by yourself.

points: The button tag makes a button
Button words should be short and clear
The words go between the opening and closing button tags

avatar.text: Brilliant work. You can now make a simple button with clear action words.
Module complete. Next, we will combine headings and paragraphs to build a simple page.

lessons.title: Headings and Paragraphs
lessons.goal: Use heading and paragraph elements to make a simple page.

avatar.text: A heading gives a page a big title. A paragraph adds a clear sentence. Let us use both to build a simple page.

flow.title: Headings tell, paragraphs explain
flow.body:
A heading is a big title. It tells the reader what the page or section is about. A paragraph is a smaller group of words. It explains an idea or gives more information. Use: -

for the biggest, most important heading -

for normal sentences A simple page often starts with one h1, then uses paragraphs to tell the story.

avatar.text: Headings tell readers what a page is about. Paragraphs explain the idea with normal sentences. See the displayed information next to understand how headings and paragraphs work together.

flow.title: Choosing the right word element
flow.body:
Use headings and paragraphs for different jobs. `

My Pets

` - `

` starts a big title - `My Pets` is the title people see - `

` closes the title `

I have a cat.

` - `

` starts a paragraph - The sentence is the content - `

` closes the paragraph A good beginner page often has one main heading first, then one or more paragraphs below it.

avatar.text: Start with one main heading. Add one or more paragraphs below it. This makes the page clear and easy to read. Take a moment to look at the examples for better understanding.

code_example.code:
My Toy Box

I have blocks, cars, and puzzles.
code_example.description: A heading element followed by a paragraph element.
code_example.explanation: The h1 element has an opening tag, title words, and a closing tag. The p element has an opening tag, sentence content, and a closing tag. Together they make a clear page title and a clear explanation.

question.question: Which tag makes the main heading?
question.explanation: The correct answer is <h1>. The h means heading, and h1 is the biggest main heading.

avatar.on_ask: Which tag makes the big title?
avatar.on_correct: Yes. `h1` is the main heading.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the heading tag.

question.question: Make a heading that says `My Favorite Activity` and a paragraph that says `I like coding.`
question.explanation: Nice. The opening h1 tag starts the heading, the title goes inside, and the closing h1 tag closes it. The opening p tag starts the paragraph, the sentence goes inside, and the closing p tag closes it.

code_example.description: A heading element followed by a paragraph element.
code_example.explanation: The title goes between h1 and slash h1. The sentence goes between p and slash p.

points: Use h1 for the main title of a page
Use p for regular sentences and explanations
Headings and paragraphs help readers understand the page quickly

avatar.text:
You can now build a simple readable page with a title and a sentence.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- Use h1 for the main title of a page
- Use p for regular sentences and explanations
- Headings and paragraphs help readers understand the page quickly
Great work. You used a heading and a paragraph together. Next, we will explore buttons, pictures, and lists.
Web pages can have buttons, pictures, and lists. Today we will meet these useful page pieces.

flow.title: More useful page pieces
flow.body: HTML has many tags because web pages need many kinds of pieces. Use: -

avatar.text: HTML has many tags because web pages need many kinds of pieces. A button invites a person to act. An image shows a picture. A list keeps related items neat and easy to read.

flow.title: Elements can have different shapes
flow.body:
Not every element is written the same way. A button wraps words: `` A list wraps list items: `
    ` `
  • Red
    • ` `
  • Blue
    • ` `
` An image is a void element: `` The image does not have words between opening and closing tags. It uses attributes like `src` and `alt` for its details.

avatar.text: Buttons hold short action words. Images use helpful details. Lists use one container with separate items inside it. Take a moment to look at the displayed information next to see how these elements are written.

code_example.code:
• Red
  • Blue
code_example.description: Several common elements, including wrapped elements and a void element.
code_example.explanation: The button wraps the word Choose and closes with </button>. The img element is void, so it uses attributes and does not need a closing tag. The ul element wraps the whole list, and each li element wraps one list item.

question.question: Which tag shows a picture?
question.explanation: The correct answer is i m g. It is short for image and is used to show a picture on the page.

avatar.on_ask: Which tag shows a picture?
avatar.on_correct: Yes. img is for images.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the short tag that sounds like image.

question.question: Which tag makes one list item?
question.explanation: The correct answer is <li>. The letters li stand for list item, which means one item inside a list.

avatar.on_ask: Which tag makes one list item?
avatar.on_correct: Correct. `li` means list item.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the tag with the letters l and i.

points: button makes something that looks pressable
img shows a picture and should include helpful alt text
ul makes a bullet list, and li makes each list item

avatar.text:
You have more page-building pieces now. Your HTML toolbox is getting nicely stocked.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- button makes something that looks pressable
- img shows a picture and should include helpful alt text
- ul makes a bullet list, and li makes each list item
Well done. You met buttons, pictures, and lists. Next, we will learn how attributes add extra details.

lessons.title: Attributes Add Details
lessons.goal: Understand that attributes give HTML elements extra information.

avatar.text: HTML elements can carry extra details. These details are called attributes.

flow.title: Attributes live in opening tags
flow.body:
An attribute is extra information inside an opening tag. It usually has a name and a value. Example: `

Hello!

` Here: - `p` is the element tag - `title` is the attribute name - `A happy note` is the attribute value Attributes help elements do more or tell the browser more details.

avatar.text: An attribute gives the browser more information about an element. It usually has a name and a value. See examples of attributes in the displayed information next to understand how they work.

flow.title: How attributes are written
flow.body:
Attributes go inside the opening tag after the tag name. Pattern: `Content` Example: `

Hello!

` Look at the parts: - `p` is the tag name - `title` is the attribute name - `=` connects the name to the value - `"A happy note"` is the value in quotes The content still goes between the opening and closing tags.

avatar.text: Attributes are placed inside an opening tag. They can name, describe, or change how an element works. The displayed information shows examples of attributes and how they are written.

code_example.code: Hello, learner!
code_example.description: Two elements use attributes in their opening tags.
code_example.explanation: The title attribute is written inside the paragraph opening tag and uses a name and value. The disabled attribute is also inside the opening button tag. Attributes belong in opening tags because they describe that element before the browser shows it.

question.question: Where do most HTML attributes go?
question.explanation:
Most attributes go inside the opening tag, like `

`.

avatar.on_ask: Where do attributes usually sit?
avatar.on_correct: Yes. Attributes live inside the opening tag.
avatar.on_wrong: Look at the start tag. That is where the attribute is placed.

question.question: Many attributes use a name and a value, like `title="Hello"`.
question.explanation: Many attributes use a name, an equals sign, and a value in quotes.

avatar.on_ask: True or false?
avatar.on_correct: Correct. Name, equals sign, value.
avatar.on_wrong: Many attributes do use a name and a value.

points: Attributes give elements extra details
Most attributes go inside the opening tag
Many attributes look like `name="value"`

avatar.text:
You learned that elements can carry extra information with attributes. Tiny details, big power.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- Attributes give elements extra details
- Most attributes go inside the opening tag
- Many attributes look like `name="value"`
Nice work. You learned how attributes add useful details. Next, we will use an attribute to make a link.

lessons.title: Links Use `href`
lessons.goal: Use the anchor element and `href` attribute to make a link.

avatar.text: A link is like a doorway on a web page. It helps a person move to another place.

flow.title: The anchor element
flow.body: A link uses the anchor element: `<.>`. The `href` attribute tells the link where to go. Example: `Visit Example` Here: - `` starts the link - `href` gives the web address - `Visit Example` is the clickable text - `` closes the link

avatar.text: The anchor element makes a link. The href attribute tells the link where it should go. Take a moment to look at the example to get a better understanding.

flow.title: Links have a place to go
flow.body: A link uses the anchor element, written with the tag name `a`. Pattern: `Clickable words` The `href` attribute is important because it holds the address. Example: `Go to Page 2` - `` opens the link and gives the address - `Go to Page 2` is the text people click - `` closes the link

avatar.text: A link uses the anchor element, written with the tag name a. It needs an address and clickable words. The clickable words should clearly tell the reader what will open. Study the displayed example next to see how the pieces fit together.

code_example.description: Two anchor elements use href to make clickable links.
code_example.explanation: Each link starts with an opening a tag that contains the href attribute. The clickable words go between the opening and closing anchor tags. The closing tag tells the browser where the link text ends.

question.question: Which attribute tells a link where to go?
question.explanation: The `href` attribute tells an anchor link where to go.

avatar.on_ask: Which attribute gives a link its place to go?
avatar.on_correct: Yes. `href` holds the link address.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the attribute used inside an anchor link.

question.question: Make a link to `https://example.com` that says `Open page`.
question.explanation: Great. The anchor element makes the link, and href gives the address.

code_example.description: A simple link with clickable words.
code_example.explanation: Put the address in `href`. Put the words people click between opening a tag and closing a tag.

avatar.before_demo: Here is a tiny link example.

points: Links use the `a` element
The `href` attribute gives the link address
The text between `` and `` is what people click

avatar.text: You made a web doorway. Links help people move from one page to another. Here are the big ideas from this lesson: - Links use the `a` element - The `href` attribute gives the link address - The text between `` and `` is what people click
Excellent. You built a simple link. Next, we will look closely at the details used by images.

lessons.title: Images Need `s r c` and `alt`
lessons.goal: Use image attributes to choose a picture and describe it.

avatar.text: Pictures need clear instructions. One detail chooses the picture, and another describes it in words.

flow.title: Image attributes
flow.body: An image uses the `` element. Important image attributes are: - `src` tells the browser which image file to show - `alt` gives words that describe the picture - `width` can tell how wide the picture should be Example: ``

avatar.text: The src attribute chooses the image file. The alt attribute gives helpful words that describe the picture.

flow.title: Images are void elements with attributes
flow.body: The image element is written with ``. It is a void element, so it does not need ``. Images need attributes to make sense. Example: `` - `src` means source. It tells the browser which image file to load. - `alt` gives helpful words that describe the image. - `width` can set the image width. Because `` is void, all the important information goes in the opening tag.

avatar.text: An image stands alone without a closing tag. Its important details are placed inside the image tag. Take a few seconds to look at the displayed information next to see how the image attributes work.

code_example.description: Two image elements use online picture URLs with `src`, `alt`, and `width`.
code_example.explanation: The s r c attribute uses an online picture URL, so the browser can load the image from the web. The alt attribute describes the picture for people who cannot see it or when the picture cannot load. The width attribute gives the browser a size to use.

question.question: Which attribute tells an image which file to show?
question.explanation: The `src` attribute tells the browser the image file source.

avatar.on_ask: Which attribute chooses the image file?
avatar.on_correct: Yes. `src` points to the image file.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the attribute that means source.

question.question: What does `alt` do for an image?
options: It describes the picture in words
question.answer: It describes the picture in words
question.explanation: The `alt` attribute gives a text description of the image.

avatar.on_ask: What job does alt do?
avatar.on_correct: Correct. alt gives helpful picture words.
avatar.on_wrong: Think about words that describe the picture.

points: The `img` element shows a picture
The `src` attribute chooses the picture file
The `alt` attribute describes the picture in words

avatar.text:
You gave pictures the details they need. A helpful image has both a file and a description.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- The `img` element shows a picture
- The `src` attribute chooses the picture file
- The `alt` attribute describes the picture in words
Fantastic. You learned how to choose and describe an image. Next, we will meet input elements.

lessons.title: Inputs Ask for Information
lessons.goal: Recognize input elements and attributes like `type`, `placeholder`, and `value`.

avatar.text: Some web pages ask people to type or choose an answer. Input elements help the page collect that information.

flow.title: Input attributes
flow.body:
An `<input>` element can make a typing box, checkbox, button, and more. Attributes tell the input what kind to be.

Useful input attributes are:

- `type` tells what kind of input it is
- `placeholder` shows a hint before typing
- `value` can give a starting value
- `id` gives the input a special name

Example:

`<input type="text" placeholder="Your name">`

avatar.text: An input element can make a typing box, checkbox, button, and more. Attributes tell the input what kind to be. Useful input attributes are: type, placeholder, value, and id.

flow.title: Inputs are also void elements
flow.body:
An input lets a person type or choose something. The input element is usually a void element.

Example:

`<input type="text" placeholder="Your name">`

Look at the attributes:

- `type="text"` makes it a typing box
- `placeholder="Your name"` shows a hint before typing

A checkbox uses a different type:

`<input type="checkbox">`

The same element can act differently because its attributes are different.

avatar.text: A text input makes a typing box. A checkbox lets a person choose an option. Attributes give each input its job. Study the displayed information next to see how input elements and their attributes are written.

code_example.code:
<label for="nameBox">Name:</label>
<input id="nameBox" type="text" placeholder="Your name">
<input type="checkbox" checked>
code_example.description: A label and two input elements with different attributes.
code_example.explanation: The label has opening and closing tags because it wraps the word Name. The input elements are void elements, so they do not close. The type attribute changes what kind of input appears, and placeholder gives hint words for the text input.

question.question: Which attribute tells an input what kind to be?
question.explanation: The `type` attribute tells an input what kind it should be.

avatar.on_ask: Which attribute chooses the kind of input?
avatar.on_correct: Yes. `type` chooses the input kind.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the attribute used in `type="text"`.

question.question: Make a text input with the placeholder `Your name`.
question.explanation: Good job. The type says it is a text box, and placeholder gives a hint.

code_example.description: A text input with a hint.
code_example.explanation: Use `type="text"` for a typing box and `placeholder` for the hint words.

avatar.before_demo: Here is a simple text input.
avatar.handoff: Now make an input with a hint.

question.question: The `placeholder` attribute can show hint words inside an input.
question.explanation: Placeholder text is a hint that appears before someone types.

avatar.on_ask: True or false?
avatar.on_correct: Correct. Placeholder gives a hint.
avatar.on_wrong: Placeholder text is a helpful hint inside the input.

points: The `input` element can ask for information
The `type` attribute chooses the kind of input
The `placeholder` attribute shows a helpful hint
Labels can give inputs friendly names

avatar.text:
You met input boxes and the attributes that help them ask clear questions.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- The `input` element can ask for information
- The `type` attribute chooses the kind of input
- The `placeholder` attribute shows a helpful hint
- Labels can give inputs friendly names
Great work. You learned how inputs collect information. Next, we will connect HTML elements to CSS selectors.

lessons.title: CSS Can Find Tags
lessons.goal: Use an HTML tag name as a CSS selector.

avatar.text: CSS changes how a page looks. First, it must choose which HTML element to style.

flow.title: Selectors choose what to style
flow.body:
CSS is the language that changes how HTML looks. Before CSS can style something, it must choose what to style. That chooser is called a selector. A tag name can become a CSS selector. HTML tag:

CSS selector: p Notice: CSS does not use angle brackets for tag selectors. It just uses the tag name.

avatar.text: CSS is the language that changes how HTML looks. Before CSS can style something, it must choose what to style. A selector tells CSS what to choose. A tag name can be used as a selector for all matching elements.

flow.title: From tag to selector
flow.body:
HTML uses angle brackets to create elements: `

Hello!

` CSS uses selectors to choose elements: `p { color: blue; }` Notice the difference: - HTML tag: `

` uses angle brackets - CSS selector: `p` does not use angle brackets When CSS sees `p`, it chooses all paragraph elements on the page. Then the style inside the braces is added to those paragraphs.

avatar.text: HTML uses tag marks to build elements. CSS uses only the tag name when it selects those elements. Look at the displayed information next to see how a tag name becomes a CSS selector.

avatar.text:
You learned the bridge from HTML to CSS: a tag can become a selector.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- CSS changes how HTML elements look
- A selector chooses which elements get the style
- A tag selector uses the tag name without angle brackets, such as p or h1
Well done. You turned a tag name into a CSS selector. Next, we will add properties and values.

lessons.title: Add Style Rules
lessons.goal: Write a CSS rule with a selector, property, and value.

avatar.text: A CSS rule chooses an element and gives it a style. Let us learn the main parts of that rule.

flow.title: A CSS rule has three helpful parts
flow.body:
A CSS rule is a style instruction. It tells the browser which element to style and what style to add.

A rule has:

- Selector: what to choose
- Property: what part to change
- Value: what to change it to

Example:

p { color: blue; }

Here, p chooses paragraphs, color changes the text color, and blue is the color we choose.

avatar.text: A selector chooses the element. A property names what will change. A value gives the new style. Take a moment to look at the displayed information next to see how a CSS rule is built.

flow.title: How to write a CSS rule
flow.body:
A CSS rule has a careful shape.

Pattern:

`selector { property: value; }`

Example:

`p { color: blue; }`

Parts:

- `p` is the selector. It chooses paragraphs.
- `{` opens the style rule.
- `color` is the property. It says what to change.
- `blue` is the value. It says the new choice.
- `;` ends that style line.
- `}` closes the style rule.

avatar.text: The selector comes first. The property and value work together to change text, backgrounds, sizes, and more. Study the displayed information to see how CSS rules are applied.

code_example.description: A complete CSS rule for button elements.
code_example.explanation: The selector button chooses button elements. The opening brace starts the rule. Each property and value pair adds one style. The semicolon ends each style line. The closing brace ends the whole rule.

question.question: In `p { color: blue; }`, which word is the property?
question.explanation: The correct answer is color. A property tells CSS what to change. Here, color means the text color will change.

avatar.on_ask: Which word is the property?
avatar.on_correct: Yes. color is what we change.
avatar.on_wrong: The property tells CSS what part to change.

question.question: In `p { color: blue; }`, which word is the value?
question.explanation: The correct answer is blue. A value is the chosen setting. Here, blue is the color we choose for the text.

avatar.on_ask: Which word is the value?
avatar.on_correct: Correct. `blue` is the chosen color value.
avatar.on_wrong: The value is the style choice after the colon.

points: A CSS rule starts with a selector
A property names what will change, such as color or background
A value is the chosen style, such as blue, yellow, or 20px

avatar.text:
You can now read CSS rules like a beginner web designer.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- A CSS rule starts with a selector
- A property names what will change, such as color or background
- A value is the chosen style, such as blue, yellow, or 20px
Excellent. You can now read the main parts of a CSS rule. Next, we will style elements with class names.

lessons.title: Class Selectors
lessons.goal: Use a class to style a group of elements.

avatar.text: A class is like a team name. Many elements can join the same style team.

flow.title: Classes are style teams
flow.body: Sometimes we do not want to style every p or every button. We may want to style only some special elements. A class helps us make a style team. In HTML, add a class name like this:

avatar.text: A class lets several elements share one style. The same class name can be added to different elements.

flow.title: Class names connect HTML and CSS
flow.body:
A class is an attribute in HTML and a selector in CSS. HTML: `

Hi!

` CSS: `.happy { color: green; }` The HTML says: this paragraph is on the happy team. The CSS says: choose every element on the happy team and make the text green. Many elements can share the same class, so classes are useful for groups.

avatar.text: A class is an attribute in HTML and a selector in CSS. HTML gives an element a class name. CSS uses a dot before that name to select every member of the class. The displayed information next to shows how a class name connects HTML and CSS.

code_example.description: A paragraph and a button share one class selector.
code_example.explanation: Both opening tags include class="bright". The CSS selector .bright starts with a dot because it chooses a class. Since both elements share that class, the yellow background is added to both.

question.question: Which CSS selector picks `class="bright"`?
question.explanation: The correct answer is .bright. Class selectors start with a dot, then the class name.

avatar.on_ask: Which selector picks the bright class?
avatar.on_correct: Yes. Classes use a dot in CSS.
avatar.on_wrong: A class selector starts with a dot.

question.question: Write a CSS selector for the class `fun`.
question.explanation: Good. .fun selects every element that has class="fun" in the HTML.

code_example.description: A class selector named fun.
code_example.explanation: Start with a dot, then write the class name.

avatar.handoff: Now write the selector for fun.

points: A class is a reusable style name
HTML writes class="name" on the element
CSS writes .name to select that class
Many elements can share the same class

avatar.text:
You can now make a style team and dress several elements the same way.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- A class is a reusable style name
- HTML writes class="name" on the element
- CSS writes .name to select that class
- Many elements can share the same class
Great work. You created a reusable style team. Next, we will give one special element its own name.

lessons.title: ID Selectors
lessons.goal: Use an ID to style one special element.

avatar.text: An ID is a special name for one element. CSS can use that name to find the element.

flow.title: IDs are special names
flow.body:
An ID is a special name for one element. Use it when one page piece needs its own name. In HTML, add an ID like this: `

My Page

` The `id` attribute gives the heading the special name `title`.

avatar.text: Use an ID when one page piece needs its own special name. An ID should not be shared across many elements.

flow.title: ID names choose one special element
flow.body:
An ID is also an attribute in HTML, but it is for one special element. HTML: `

My Page

` CSS: `#title { color: blue; }` The HTML gives the heading a special ID name: `title`. The CSS uses `#title` to choose that one element. Remember: - Class uses a dot: `.happy` - ID uses a hash sign: `#title`

avatar.text: HTML adds the ID name to the element. CSS uses a hash sign before the name to select that special element. Learn how to use an ID name in the displayed information.

code_example.description: One heading uses an ID selector for a special style.
code_example.explanation: The h1 opening tag includes id="mainTitle". The CSS selector #mainTitle starts with # because it chooses an ID. This style is meant for that one special heading.

question.question: Which CSS selector picks `id="mainTitle"`?
question.explanation: The correct answer is #mainTitle. ID selectors start with #, then the id name.

avatar.on_ask: Which selector picks the id?
avatar.on_correct: Correct. IDs use `#` in CSS.
avatar.on_wrong: An id selector starts with `#`.

question.question: Which one is best for a group of elements?
question.explanation: The correct answer is class. A class is best for groups because many elements can share the same class name.

avatar.on_ask: Which one is best for a group?
avatar.on_correct: Yes. A class is a style team.
avatar.on_wrong: A class can be shared by many elements.

points: An id gives one element a special name
HTML writes id="name" on the element
CSS writes #name to select that id
Use class for groups and id for one special element

avatar.text:
You now know three ways to choose elements: tag selectors, class selectors, and id selectors.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- An id gives one element a special name
- HTML writes id="name" on the element
- CSS writes #name to select that id
- Use class for groups and id for one special element
Brilliant. You now know tag, class, and id selectors. Next, we will place CSS inside a style element.
CSS needs a place to live inside an HTML page. The style element gives it a home.

flow.title: The style element holds CSS
flow.body:
HTML can hold CSS inside a <style> element. The style element is like a small art corner for the page.

Inside <style>, we write CSS rules:

<style>
  p { color: blue; }
</style>

The browser reads the HTML elements, then reads the CSS rules, then shows the page with the styles added.

avatar.text: The style element holds CSS rules. The browser reads those rules and uses them to decorate the page. Study the example next to see how a style element is written.

flow.title: The style element is not visible text
flow.body:
The `<style>` element holds CSS rules inside an HTML page.

It has an opening tag and a closing tag:

`<style>`
`p { color: blue; }`
`</style>`

The CSS inside `<style>` is not shown as normal page words. The browser reads it as instructions for how the page should look.

So the page has two kinds of instructions:

- HTML elements for structure
- CSS rules inside `<style>` for decoration

avatar.text: HTML builds the page pieces. CSS inside the style element changes how those pieces look. Take a moment to look at the example next to see how a style element is written and how it is not visible text.

code_example.code:
My Garden

Flowers are bright.
code_example.description: HTML elements are built first, then CSS rules inside style decorate them.
code_example.explanation: The h1 and p elements are normal HTML elements with opening and closing tags. The style element also has an opening and closing tag. Inside it, h1 chooses headings and p chooses paragraphs, then the color property changes their text colors.

question.question: Which HTML element can hold CSS?
question.explanation: The correct answer is <style>. CSS rules can be placed inside the style element.

avatar.on_ask: Which element holds CSS?
avatar.on_correct: Yes. CSS can go inside `<style>`.
avatar.on_wrong: Look for the tag named style.

question.question: Inside a style tag, make all paragraphs red.
question.explanation: Great. The style tag holds the CSS, p chooses paragraphs, and color: red; makes paragraph text red.

code_example.description: A style tag with a paragraph rule.
code_example.explanation: Put the CSS rule between `<style>` and `</style>`.

avatar.before_demo: Here is a style tag with one rule.

points: The style element can hold CSS rules
CSS rules inside style can choose and decorate HTML elements
The browser combines HTML structure and CSS style to show the final page

avatar.text:
You learned where CSS can live when it is written inside an HTML page.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- The style element can hold CSS rules
- CSS rules inside style can choose and decorate HTML elements
- The browser combines HTML structure and CSS style to show the final page
Excellent. You placed CSS inside an HTML page. Next, we will combine everything in one small project.

lessons.title: Final Styled Page
lessons.goal: Build a small page using elements, selectors, and styles.

avatar.text: Now we will combine HTML and CSS to build a small styled page.

flow.title: Build, choose, style
flow.body:
A finished beginner page has two big jobs:

1. HTML builds the pieces.
2. CSS chooses pieces and styles them.

We can choose elements in three beginner-friendly ways:

- Tag selector: h1 chooses all h1 headings
- Class selector: .happy chooses the happy team
- ID selector: #title chooses one special element

When these work together, a plain page becomes a styled page.

avatar.text: A finished beginner page has two big jobs: 1, HTML builds the pieces. 2, CSS chooses pieces and styles them. HTML creates the page pieces. CSS chooses those pieces and changes their appearance.

points: A tag is written with a left angle bracket, a tag name, and a right angle bracket
Many elements have an opening tag, content, and a closing tag with a slash
Void tags like `img`, `br`, and `input` do not need closing tags
Attributes add extra details inside opening tags
Links use `href` to know where to go
Images use `src` for the picture file and `alt` for helpful picture words
Inputs use attributes like `type` and `placeholder` to ask for information
CSS selectors choose which HTML elements to style
Tag selectors use tag names like h1, p, and button without angle brackets
Class selectors use a dot, like .happy, and can style a group
ID selectors use #, like #title, and style one special element
Styles can be added inside the <style> element

avatar.text:
You built your web map: tags make elements, closing tags use slashes, void tags stand alone, attributes add details, selectors choose elements, and CSS makes the page shine.

Here are the big ideas from this lesson:
- A tag is written with a left angle bracket, a tag name, and a right angle bracket
- Many elements have an opening tag, content, and a closing tag with a slash
- Void tags like `img`, `br`, and `input` do not need closing tags
- Attributes add extra details inside opening tags
- Links use `href` to know where to go
- Images use `src` for the picture file and `alt` for helpful picture words
- Inputs use attributes like `type` and `placeholder` to ask for information
- CSS selectors choose which HTML elements to style
- Tag selectors use tag names like h1, p, and button without angle brackets
- Class selectors use a dot, like .happy, and can style a group
- ID selectors use #, like #title, and style one special element
- Styles can be added inside the <style> element
Course complete. You can now build page pieces, add details, choose elements, and style them with CSS.
